metadata.note: Southern Pacific's Coast Division between San Jose and Santa Barbara, drawn as the nine stages in which it was actually built, so the map shows the railhead creeping south. This layer exists to fill a hole: before it, nothing on the map served San Luis Obispo, Salinas, Paso Robles or Santa Maria between the 1870 end of sf_san_jose_railroad.geojson and the 1937 start of southern_pacific_coast_daylight.geojson. In 1897 - the year that prompted this layer - San Luis Obispo sat on a Southern Pacific stub running south from San Francisco as far as Surf, and on the Pacific Coast Railway's narrow gauge (pacific_coast_railway.geojson). Every feature is drawn from its opening year to 1971, when Southern Pacific handed intercity passenger service to Amtrak; the named streamliners that later ran this same iron are drawn separately in southern_pacific_coast_daylight.geojson and amtrak.geojson, so those features deliberately overlap this one. LA - Santa Barbara (opened August 1887 via the Santa Clara River valley) is NOT included here.
metadata.source: OpenStreetMap relations 4515581 (UP Coast Subdivision) and 4525173 (UP Santa Barbara Subdivision) for geometry; Southern Pacific 'Seventy-Five Years of Progress 1869-1944' (cprr.org), Wikipedia 'Coast Line (California)' and 'San Luis Obispo station', and the Monterey County Historical Society's 'Railroads of the Central Coast' for dates.
metadata.geometry_quality: Traced from present-day OSM track. San Jose - San Luis Obispo comes out at 200.9 mi against a documented Southern Pacific mileage of about 201 mi (SF-SLO 248.3 mi less SF-San Jose 47 mi), and San Luis Obispo - Guadalupe at 24.2 mi against a documented 25 mi. Straight-line bridging totals about 2.5 mi, all of it between Guadalupe and Surf. The one place the drawn alignment is later than the era shown is the San Jose end, which uses Southern Pacific's 1935 line around downtown San Jose.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: No 19th- or 20th-century Southern Pacific timetable was consulted: every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh here is an estimate. The Templeton/Santa Margarita railhead date (1886 vs 1889) and the San Luis Obispo first-train date (May 4 vs May 5 1894) are both unresolved conflicts between sources. The 'about 80 miles' usually quoted for the Surf - Santa Barbara gap does not match the 67.7 mi traced.

segments.note: Southern Pacific reached Gilroy on March 13 1869, the first stage of the Coast Division south of San Jose. Stub-end era. Until the Surf - Santa Barbara gap closed there was no through Coast Line train; service was San Francisco - railhead locals and mixed trains, with the far end connecting to Pacific Coast Steamship sailings. headway_min is an estimate - no 19th-century timetable was consulted.
sources: Segment-level: opening date March 13 1869 from Southern Pacific's own 'Seventy-Five Years of Progress' chronology; headway and speed are estimates.

segments.note: Through Coast Line era. Regular San Francisco - Los Angeles passenger service began March 31 1901 once ballasting of the new Surf - Santa Barbara line was finished. Named trains over this corridor included the Shore Line Limited (March 1 1906 - September 15 1931), the Coast Line Limited and the Lark overnight train. headway_min is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: opening date March 13 1869 from Southern Pacific's own 'Seventy-Five Years of Progress' chronology; headway and speed are estimates.

The named trains themselves are drawn separately in southern_pacific_coast_daylight.geojson and amtrak.geojson. headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: Track reached Surf, on the beach at the mouth of the Santa Ynez River, in 1896; the river bridge was finished early in 1897 and Surf went into the timetable. For five years Surf was the end of the line, and San Luis Obispo an intermediate stop on a stub from San Francisco. Stub-end era. Until the Surf - Santa Barbara gap closed there was no through Coast Line train; service was San Francisco - railhead locals and mixed trains, with the far end connecting to Pacific Coast Steamship sailings. headway_min is an estimate - no 19th-century timetable was consulted.
